subject: Inference networking options: peering vs service-endpoint vs s2s VPN

Subject: Onboarding Redwood Private — connectivity options & constraints

Hi Marcus,

Thanks for the intro call earlier. We're kicking off the network workstream for our Redwood Private pilot and want guidance on which connectivity option makes sense for OrchidHealth. High level constraints:

- VPC in us-east-1 (10.10.0.0/16), single account owned by OrchidHealth; also a co-lo datacenter in NYC with existing SD-WAN.
- Compliance: SOC2 + HIPAA; required network separation and ability to produce audit logs for flow records.
- Expected production load: ~150 RPS at peak, bursts to 300, typical inference payloads small.
- Latency: <40ms one-way desirable for our UI flows.
- Security: mTLS for mutual auth preferred; ability to restrict IPs and enforce security groups.

Options on the table: VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink (service endpoints), or site-to-site VPN (strongSwan/SD-WAN). We also have a third-party Managed VPN partner (EdgeConnect) copied here.

Attached is our VPC CIDR sheet and a quick network diagram. Can you outline tradeoffs and your recommended path (including fallback plan)? If useful we can schedule a 30m deep-dive.

Thanks — Sonia

Sonia — thanks for the detailed notes and attachments, this is helpful. High level summary and tradeoffs below; follow-up with a recommended pilot approach at the bottom.

Quick TL;DR: PrivateLink (service endpoint) + small s2s VPN fallback is the lowest operational blast radius and easiest path to meet compliance. Peering can work but has important caveats (cross-account limitations, transitive routing, CIDR clash risk).

Short pros/cons:
- VPC Peering:
  - Pros: low latency, native L3 routing, no additional hop through a managed endpoint.
  - Cons: must ensure non-overlapping CIDRs, does not scale transitively (Redwood can't peer to multiple customer VPCs and have them talk through a single hop without extra infra), cross-account peering requires careful IAM and route-control. Harder to lock down at service level (IP granularity).
- PrivateLink / Service Endpoint (our recommended default):
  - Pros: strong isolation (service endpoints are per-customer), fine-grained access via endpoint policies and SGs, central control of TLS termination options, works cross-account without VPC CIDR changes. Simpler audit logging and easier to reason about security boundaries.
  - Cons: additional networking hop (NLB -> ENI -> customer), small added latency (usually single-digit ms), needs support for preservation of client IP if you require it (we can preserve via proxy/NLB config but needs explicit config).
- Site-to-site VPN:
  - Pros: quick to stand up, supports on-prem connectivity to co-lo, useful as fallback/DMZ for admin traffic.
  - Cons: typically higher and variable latency, can be less reliable unless provisioned HA, requires key/ASN coordination with your edge team.

Pilot recommendation (practical):
1) Primary: PrivateLink endpoint from your VPC to Redwood Private. Configure endpoint policy to restrict to specific subnets and IAM principal(s). Use mTLS between Redwood and your app; we support client cert-based auth.
2) Backup: Establish an HA S2S VPN between your SD-WAN / co-lo edge and our customer VPN endpoint (used only if PrivateLink is unavailable or for initial bootstrap).
3) Avoid peering unless you need raw L3 performance and can commit to non-overlapping CIDRs and ongoing route management. If you choose peering, we recommend a short pilot with explicit CIDR reservation and conservative route propagation.

Action items for the network deep-dive:
- Sonia / Orchid: confirm whether you require preservation of the original client IP for application-level logging (yes/no).
- Provide ASN(s) and public IP blocks for the co-lo/SD-WAN for VPN setup.
- We (Redwood): will prepare endpoint policy examples + NLB config notes and a runbook for VPN termination.

If that matches your expectations I can loop Karthik for the kernel/runtime impact (perf/latency numbers) and Lauren for compliance/audit artifacts. Suggest a 30m call tomorrow to walk the diagram.

— Marcus

Adding a few technical details from infra/runtime perspective. I agree with Marcus' recommendation but want to call out the perf and ops implications so Orchid can make an informed choice.

Performance notes:
- PrivateLink latency: expect +3–8ms on top of baseline RTT in us-east-1 for our NLB -> ENI path under normal load. For 150–300 RPS this is negligible; for extremely latency-sensitive <10ms apps peering might be required.
- Throughput: our NLB + service architecture supports your peak without additional capacity if we provision target groups correctly; we recommend initial burst headroom of 2x.
- Client IP preservation: if Orchid needs source IP intact for app logs we can enable X-Forwarded-For and preserve via proxy. True source IP at L4 only possible with peering or if we terminate TLS at the customer side (less common).

Operational controls & security:
- Endpoint policies + security groups + mTLS give the strongest defense-in-depth. PrivateLink allows us to provide per-account endpoint principals for least privilege.
- Flow logs: to meet SOC2/HIPAA evidence, we can provide VPC Flow Logs and our access logs. We'll include cross-account read-only CloudWatch/CloudTrail artifacts or export to your log bucket as part of the onboarding runbook.
- Failover plan: configure health checks in the NLB and add route priority changes in your SD-WAN to route to VPN in case of endpoint outage.

Peering caveats to reiterate:
- No transitive routing: if Orchid later wants to extend a single peering into multiple accounts or a transit VPC, additional networking (transit gateway) will be required.
- IP exhaustion risk: peering makes CIDR planning critical — from your sheet the 10.10.0.0/16 is fine but leaves little wiggle room across dev/prod if you want multiple peers.

Recommendation for the pilot (technical checklist):
- Provision a PrivateLink endpoint in a test subnet; attach least-privilege endpoint policy.
- Redwood: provide example NLB config + cert rollover schedule.
- Orchid: share ASN and two public IPs for VPN termination (for HA) and confirm log bucket details.
- Schedule a 30m cutover window for testing (we'll run a perf sweep during low-traffic window).

I'll draft the NLB/endpoint policy snippets after the call and include sample commands for your infra team.

— Karthik
